title: Rate limits & Org/Project keys demo with Emeritus Health
summary: Redwood AE + SE demo of rate limiting, quotas, and org/project key controls for Emeritus Health. Discussed hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs, per-project throttles, key rotation, SSO and audit logs. Agreed pilot scope: 3-week test using org+project keys, run traffic generator and collect latency/cost metrics.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, I'm joined by Luis, our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Anita (Emeritus): Doing well, thanks. Excited to see how you handle rate limits — we have some strict multi-tenant requirements.
[00:18] Luis (Redwood SE): Quick agenda: we'll walk through the console org/project keys model, demo rate limit config per project, show quota reporting in Console/Optimize, and then cover security pieces like key rotation and audit logs. We'll leave time for Qs.
[00:30] Rajiv (Emeritus): Sounds good. For context, we run a gateway that fans out to different product teams, so we need per-team quotas and hard throttles during incidents.
[00:40] Maya: Great, we'll demo exactly that. One note, apologies — Fireflies sometimes munges a few words, so if anything looks odd in the transcript I will clarify.
[00:50] Luis: Jumping into the Console — here is the org page, you can see project list. Each project gets its own project API key. You can attach rate-limit policies to each key or to the route.
[01:10] Anita: So keys are our main tenant isolation primitive? We prefer to keep identity at the project level rather than single global key.
[01:18] Luis: Yes, exactly. Org keys are for org-level admin operations, project keys are what services use. You can also map SSO groups to projects for RBAC.
[01:30] Maya: A common pattern we recommend is project keys per team, with a shared org admin key for infra. That lets you throttle a single team without affecting others.
[01:42] Rajiv: How are rate limits enforced? Token-based? Requests per minute?
[01:48] Luis: You can do both. We support per-token (per-input token) and per-request ceilings. The Console lets you set sliding window RPS, burst capacity, and token budgets. For example we set a 10qps burst with 5qps sustained, plus a token-per-minute budget for cost control.
[02:10] Anita: Ok. What happens on a throttle? Do requests queue, or do they fail?
[02:16] Luis: By default they return 429s. You can configure graceful degradation rules — e.g., route to a cheaper model variant or to cached responses. There's also a backoff header to help clients retry safely.
[02:30] Hannah (Emeritus): Speaking of caching, does KV cache get shared across projects? We don't want cross-tenant leakage.
[02:38] Luis: Good question. KV/ prefix caches are scoped to project keys — no cross-tenant sharing. There's also an option to persist per-project caches to avoid cold-starts.
[02:52] Maya: For your SRE flow, Rajiv, you can also set an org-level fallback that in outage sends requests to a dedicated standby model for critical routes.
[03:05] Rajiv: Nice. On the KMS front — can keys be customer-managed? We need HSM-backed rotation.
[03:12] Luis: Yes, Private deployments support customer KMS/HSM. For Hosted we support BYOK via Cloud KMS integrations and automated rotation policies.
[03:24] Anita: Audit trails: we need full immutable logs for access to keys and who changed rate limits.
[03:30] Luis: Console audit logs include actor, timestamp, before/after for policy changes. For Private deployments we can ship logs to your SIEM.
[03:42] Maya: Quick demo of quota reporting in Optimize — you can see per-project consumption, token breakdown, and cost per 1k tokens. This helps you enforce budgets per product team.
[03:58] Anita: Is there a way to automatically cap spend if a team exceeds budget?
[04:03] Luis: Yes, you can set a hard quota which will stop issuance of tokens for that project, and an alerting policy that pages the oncall via webhook.
[04:16] Rajiv: Real world question: we have bursty traffic during morning digest job — could bursts spike cost massively?
[04:24] Maya: Two mitigations: 1) Use caching for static prompts, 2) pin a cheaper quantized variant for high-throughput routes, and 3) use burst budgeting where bursts draw from a limited credit pool.
[04:40] Hannah: On SSO— we use Okta and SAML. Does Redwood support SAML SSO and group sync?
[04:47] Luis: Yes, SAML and SCIM group sync are supported. You can map Okta groups to Redwood project roles.
[04:55] Anita: Any constraints around VPC Private deployments? We may need an air-gapped instance.
[05:02] Luis: Private on-prem supports air-gapped installs; the control plane can be run in your VPC. Some features like hosted benchmark telemetry are opt-in and can be disabled.
[05:14] Maya: Back to rate limits — show example: attaching policy to project 'DigestTeam' — setting 100k tokens/day, 50 rps peak, 10 rps sustained.
[05:30] Luis: We apply quotas at the gateway layer and enforce at the runtime; enforcement is fast (<10ms additional latency normally) — but of course depends on your infra and whether you use dedicated pools.
[05:44] Rajiv: Have you measured p99 extra latency for throttling?
[05:48] Luis: In hosted tests we've seen p99 add ~8-12ms, dedicated with colocated routing is lower. We can share the benchmark sheet.
[05:58] Anita: We'll definitely want the benchmark sheet.
[06:02] Maya: Note: I'll send the benchmark spreadsheet and the security pack.
[06:06] Rajiv: On key rotation frequency — we have a policy to rotate every 30 days. Does Redwood support automated rotation and key revocation without downtime?
[06:14] Luis: Yes, key rotation can be staged: create new key, update projects, then revoke old key. We support key aliases so you can rotate without needing to update clients if you manage mapping in your gateway. For BYOK there might be a short window during rotation but no planned downtime.
[06:32] Hannah: What about audit of API key usage per user? We need to link API calls back to identity.
[06:39] Luis: You can attach a caller identity header from your gateway that Redwood copies into logs; in Private deployments you can use mutual TLS to authenticate service-to-service.
[06:52] Anita: Any competitor differentiators you want to highlight?
[06:56] Maya: Two things — production-first controls (policy attach per-project with observable SLOs) and unified runtime (same config works hosted or private). We also have built-in Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization to reduce unit cost.
[07:12] Rajiv: Ok, for pilot scope — we'd want 3 projects (DigestTeam, SearchTeam, Alerts), run synthetic load for two weeks and capture latency and cost. We'll check security pack and SOC2 attestations.
[07:24] Luis: That works. We'll provide a test plan template.
[07:28] Anita: Are there any hard limits on number of projects or keys? We're thinking ~150 internal teams.
[07:34] Luis: No hard software limit; we've supported thousands. For very large counts we recommend using organization-level routing policies and hierarchical quotas.
[07:46] Maya: Ok, quick wrap. I'll recap next steps.
[07:50] Hannah: Quick question — can we rotate keys daily if required?
[07:54] Luis: Technically yes; but operationally we'd recommend weekly or policy-based rotation to avoid client churn. Also we can automate via SCIM or API.
[08:06] Maya: Great. We're at the last 2 minutes so recap: we'll send security pack + SOC2, benchmark spreadsheet, and a pilot test plan. You'll get a draft contract if you want dedicated capacity pricing after pilot.
[08:20] Rajiv: Thanks.
[08:22] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with docs and a proposed pilot kickoff time.
[08:28] [call ends — 42 minutes total]
